title: Shannon Entropy
description: Shannon entropy H(X) quantifies uncertainty in a random variable. Covers the formula in bits and nats, maximum/minimum entropy cases, binary entropy, axiomatic derivation, joint and conditional entropy, chain rule, and the source coding theorem.

blocks.content: Shannon entropy is the foundational quantity of information theory. It measures the average uncertainty (or surprise) associated with a random variable's outcomes. Introduced by Claude Shannon in 1948, it provides the theoretical limit for lossless data compression and underlies virtually every concept in information theory.
Definition — Bits and Nats

For a discrete random variable X with probability mass function p(x), the Shannon entropy is defined as H(X) = -Σ_x p(x) log p(x). The choice of logarithm base determines the unit: log base 2 gives bits (the natural unit for binary communication), log base e gives nats, and log base 10 gives hartleys. The convention 0 · log 0 = 0 handles zero-probability events (confirmed by the limit lim_{p→0} p log p = 0).

blocks.title: Entropy as Average Surprise
blocks.content: The surprise (self-information) of an event with probability p is -log₂ p bits. A coin flip with p=0.5 yields 1 bit of surprise; a 1-in-1024 event yields 10 bits. Entropy is the expectation of surprise: H(X) = E[-log p(X)].
Maximum and Minimum Entropy

Entropy is maximized by the uniform distribution: for a variable with n outcomes, H(X) ≤ log₂ n bits, with equality when p(x) = 1/n for all x. Entropy is minimized (H = 0) for a deterministic variable — one outcome has probability 1 and all others 0. These bounds make entropy a natural measure of 'randomness' or 'flatness' of a distribution.

import numpy as np
from scipy.stats import entropy as scipy_entropy
from collections import Counter

# --- Entropy from scratch ---
def entropy_bits(probs):
    """Shannon entropy in bits. Accepts array of probabilities."""
    probs = np.asarray(probs, dtype=float)
    probs = probs[probs > 0]  # drop zero-probability events
    return -np.sum(probs * np.log2(probs))

# --- Entropy from counts (strings, tokens, etc.) ---
def entropy_from_counts(counts):
    counts = np.asarray(counts, dtype=float)
    probs = counts / counts.sum()
    return entropy_bits(probs)

# --- Verify against scipy ---
uniform4 = [0.25, 0.25, 0.25, 0.25]
biased   = [0.7, 0.2, 0.08, 0.02]

print(f"Uniform (4 outcomes): {entropy_bits(uniform4):.4f} bits  (max = log2(4) = 2.0)")
print(f"Biased distribution:  {entropy_bits(biased):.4f} bits")
print(f"Scipy check (nats→bits): {scipy_entropy(biased) / np.log(2):.4f} bits")

# --- Entropy of English text (letter frequencies) ---
text = "the quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog"
counts = Counter(c for c in text if c != ' ')
print(f"\nLetter entropy of sample text: {entropy_from_counts(list(counts.values())):.4f} bits")
print(f"Maximum possible (26 letters): {np.log2(26):.4f} bits")
Binary Entropy Function

For a Bernoulli(p) random variable (a biased coin), the entropy is the binary entropy function H(p) = -p log₂ p - (1-p) log₂(1-p). This function is symmetric around p = 0.5, achieves its maximum of 1 bit at p = 0.5 (fair coin), and equals 0 at p = 0 and p = 1 (deterministic outcomes). The binary entropy function appears throughout information theory as the fundamental building block for more complex expressions.

import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

def binary_entropy(p):
    """H(p) = -p log2 p - (1-p) log2 (1-p), in bits."""
    p = np.asarray(p, dtype=float)
    # Numerically safe: handle p=0 and p=1
    result = np.zeros_like(p)
    mask = (p > 0) & (p < 1)
    pm = p[mask]
    result[mask] = -pm * np.log2(pm) - (1 - pm) * np.log2(1 - pm)
    return result

p_vals = np.linspace(0, 1, 1000)
h_vals = binary_entropy(p_vals)

plt.figure(figsize=(7, 4))
plt.plot(p_vals, h_vals, color='steelblue', linewidth=2)
plt.axvline(0.5, color='tomato', linestyle='--', alpha=0.7, label='p=0.5 (max)')
plt.axhline(1.0, color='gray', linestyle=':', alpha=0.5)
plt.xlabel('p (probability of outcome 1)')
plt.ylabel('H(p) in bits')
plt.title('Binary Entropy Function H(p)')
plt.legend()
plt.tight_layout()
plt.savefig('binary_entropy.png', dpi=150)
plt.show()
print(f"Maximum at p=0.5: H(0.5) = {binary_entropy(np.array([0.5]))[0]:.4f} bits")
print(f"At p=0.9: H(0.9) = {binary_entropy(np.array([0.9]))[0]:.4f} bits")
Axiomatic Derivation

Shannon proved that H is the unique function (up to a positive constant) satisfying three natural axioms: (1) Continuity — H(p₁, ..., pₙ) is continuous in all pᵢ; (2) Symmetry — H is invariant to permutations of outcomes; (3) Monotonicity — H(1/n, ..., 1/n) is monotonically increasing in n (more equally-likely outcomes → more uncertainty). These axioms uniquely determine H(X) = -K Σ p(x) log p(x) for some constant K > 0 (which fixes the unit).

import numpy as np
from scipy.optimize import minimize
from scipy.special import entr  # entr(p) = -p * log(p)

def entropy_bits(probs):
    probs = np.asarray(probs, dtype=float)
    return np.sum(entr(probs)) / np.log(2)

n = 6  # number of outcomes

# Maximize entropy via constrained optimization
def neg_entropy(p):
    p = np.clip(p, 1e-12, 1)
    return -entropy_bits(p)

constraints = {'type': 'eq', 'fun': lambda p: np.sum(p) - 1}
bounds = [(1e-8, 1)] * n
p0 = np.ones(n) / n + np.random.dirichlet(np.ones(n)) * 0.01
p0 /= p0.sum()

result = minimize(neg_entropy, p0, method='SLSQP',
                  bounds=bounds, constraints=constraints)
optimal_p = result.x

print("Maximum entropy distribution (n=6):")
print(np.round(optimal_p, 4))  # should be ~uniform
print(f"Achieved entropy: {entropy_bits(optimal_p):.4f} bits")
print(f"Uniform entropy:  {np.log2(n):.4f} bits  (= log2({n}))")

# Show that ANY non-uniform distribution has lower entropy
for name, p in [("skewed", [0.5,0.2,0.1,0.1,0.05,0.05]),
                ("concentrated", [0.9,0.02,0.02,0.02,0.02,0.02]),
                ("uniform", [1/6]*6)]:
    print(f"  {name:15s}: H = {entropy_bits(p):.4f} bits")
Joint and Conditional Entropy

For a pair of random variables (X, Y), the joint entropy is H(X,Y) = -Σ_{x,y} p(x,y) log p(x,y). The conditional entropy H(Y|X) measures remaining uncertainty in Y after observing X: H(Y|X) = Σ_x p(x) H(Y|X=x) = -Σ_{x,y} p(x,y) log p(y|x). Conditioning always reduces entropy: H(Y|X) ≤ H(Y), with equality if and only if X and Y are independent.

The chain rule factorizes joint entropy: H(X,Y) = H(X) + H(Y|X). This extends to n variables: H(X₁,...,Xₙ) = Σᵢ H(Xᵢ | X₁,...,Xᵢ₋₁). Subadditivity states H(X,Y) ≤ H(X) + H(Y), with equality iff X ⊥ Y.
Differential Entropy for Continuous Variables

For a continuous random variable X with density f(x), differential entropy is h(X) = -∫ f(x) log f(x) dx. Unlike discrete entropy, differential entropy can be negative (e.g., Uniform(0,1/2) has h = -1 bit). It is not invariant to changes of variables: h(aX) = h(X) + log|a|. The Gaussian N(μ, σ²) maximizes differential entropy among all distributions with fixed variance: h(N) = (1/2) log(2πeσ²) nats.

blocks.title: Differential Entropy Pitfall
blocks.content: Differential entropy is NOT the limit of discrete entropy as bin width → 0. It can be negative and is not invariant to reparametrization, unlike discrete entropy. Use it for comparing distributions with the same support, not as an absolute measure.
Source Coding Theorem and Huffman Codes

Shannon's source coding theorem (1948) establishes that the minimum expected code length for lossless compression of a source X is bounded below by H(X) bits. More precisely, for any uniquely decodable code, E[L] ≥ H(X), and there exist codes (Huffman codes) achieving E[L] < H(X) + 1. This means entropy is the fundamental limit for lossless compression.

import numpy as np
from heapq import heappush, heappop
from collections import defaultdict

def entropy_bits(probs):
    probs = np.asarray(probs, dtype=float)
    probs = probs[probs > 0]
    return -np.sum(probs * np.log2(probs))

def huffman_codes(probs, symbols=None):
    """Build Huffman code and return code lengths."""
    if symbols is None:
        symbols = list(range(len(probs)))
    heap = [[p, [s, ""]] for p, s in zip(probs, symbols)]
    import heapq
    heapq.heapify(heap)
    while len(heap) > 1:
        lo = heapq.heappop(heap)
        hi = heapq.heappop(heap)
        for pair in lo[1:]:
            pair[1] = '0' + pair[1]
        for pair in hi[1:]:
            pair[1] = '1' + pair[1]
        heapq.heappush(heap, [lo[0] + hi[0]] + lo[1:] + hi[1:])
    return {sym: code for sym, code in heap[0][1:]}

# Example: English-like distribution
probs = [0.30, 0.25, 0.20, 0.12, 0.08, 0.05]
symbols = ['a', 'b', 'c', 'd', 'e', 'f']

H = entropy_bits(probs)
codes = huffman_codes(probs, symbols)
code_lengths = {s: len(c) for s, c in codes.items()}
expected_length = sum(p * code_lengths[s] for p, s in zip(probs, symbols))

print(f"Shannon entropy H(X) = {H:.4f} bits")
print(f"Expected Huffman code length = {expected_length:.4f} bits")
print(f"Redundancy = {expected_length - H:.4f} bits  (always < 1)")
print("\nCode table:")
for s, p in zip(symbols, probs):
    print(f"  '{s}': p={p:.2f}  code={codes[s]}  len={code_lengths[s]}")

rows: No finite maximum for fixed mean

blocks.content: Key Properties Summary

items: Non-negativity: H(X) ≥ 0, with H(X) = 0 iff X is deterministic
Maximum: H(X) ≤ log₂ n for n-outcome variable, achieved by uniform distribution
Continuity: H is continuous in all probabilities
Symmetry: H is invariant to relabeling of outcomes
Additivity: H(X,Y) = H(X) + H(Y) when X ⊥ Y
Chain rule: H(X,Y) = H(X) + H(Y|X) = H(Y) + H(X|Y)
Data processing: H(f(X)) ≤ H(X) for any function f
Concavity: H is a concave function of the probability distribution

blocks.title: Practical Rule of Thumb
blocks.content: Entropy tells you the minimum average number of yes/no questions needed to identify the outcome. A source with entropy H bits requires at least H binary questions on average — this is exactly what an optimal binary code achieves.

Shannon entropy underpins lossless compression (Huffman, arithmetic coding), mutual information, KL divergence, and the capacity of communication channels. Understanding it deeply is prerequisite for every other concept in information theory and modern machine learning theory.

title: Joint Entropy and Conditional Entropy
description: Joint entropy H(X,Y) and conditional entropy H(Y|X) formalized. Covers the chain rule, subadditivity, conditioning reduces entropy, mutual information, the data processing inequality, and entropy of deterministic functions.

blocks.content: Moving beyond a single random variable, joint entropy and conditional entropy capture the information structure of multiple variables. These quantities are the building blocks for mutual information, which quantifies statistical dependence, and underlie the chain rule that decomposes complex joint distributions into a sequence of conditional ones.
Joint Entropy H(X,Y)

For a pair (X, Y) with joint distribution p(x, y), the joint entropy is H(X,Y) = -Σ_{x∈X, y∈Y} p(x,y) log p(x,y). It measures the total uncertainty in the pair. Joint entropy satisfies max(H(X), H(Y)) ≤ H(X,Y) ≤ H(X) + H(Y). The lower bound is tight when Y is a deterministic function of X (or vice versa); the upper bound is tight when X and Y are independent.

blocks.title: Intuition for Joint Entropy
blocks.content: H(X,Y) is the number of bits needed to describe the pair (X,Y) simultaneously. It cannot exceed H(X)+H(Y) — knowing two things together is never harder than knowing them separately — and it cannot be less than knowing either one alone.

import numpy as np
from itertools import product

def joint_entropy(joint_dist):
    """H(X,Y) from a 2D joint probability matrix."""
    pxy = np.asarray(joint_dist, dtype=float)
    assert np.isclose(pxy.sum(), 1.0), "Probabilities must sum to 1"
    pxy_flat = pxy.flatten()
    pxy_flat = pxy_flat[pxy_flat > 0]
    return -np.sum(pxy_flat * np.log2(pxy_flat))

def marginal_entropy(joint_dist, axis):
    """H(X) or H(Y) from the joint distribution."""
    pxy = np.asarray(joint_dist, dtype=float)
    marginal = pxy.sum(axis=axis)
    marginal = marginal[marginal > 0]
    return -np.sum(marginal * np.log2(marginal))

def conditional_entropy(joint_dist):
    """H(Y|X) = H(X,Y) - H(X)."""
    return joint_entropy(joint_dist) - marginal_entropy(joint_dist, axis=1)

# Example 1: independent X, Y  (pxy = px * py)
px = np.array([0.5, 0.5])
py = np.array([0.6, 0.4])
pxy_indep = np.outer(px, py)

HXY = joint_entropy(pxy_indep)
HX  = marginal_entropy(pxy_indep, axis=1)
HY  = marginal_entropy(pxy_indep, axis=0)
print("Independent case:")
print(f"  H(X)   = {HX:.4f}  H(Y)   = {HY:.4f}")
print(f"  H(X,Y) = {HXY:.4f}  (should equal H(X)+H(Y) = {HX+HY:.4f})")

# Example 2: correlated X, Y
pxy_corr = np.array([[0.4, 0.1], [0.1, 0.4]])
HXY2 = joint_entropy(pxy_corr)
HX2  = marginal_entropy(pxy_corr, axis=1)
HY2  = marginal_entropy(pxy_corr, axis=0)
print("\nCorrelated case:")
print(f"  H(X,Y) = {HXY2:.4f} < H(X)+H(Y) = {HX2+HY2:.4f}")
Conditional Entropy H(Y|X)

The conditional entropy H(Y|X) = Σ_x p(x) H(Y|X=x) = -Σ_{x,y} p(x,y) log p(y|x) measures the remaining uncertainty in Y after observing X. It is the average entropy of the conditional distribution p(y|x) weighted by p(x). Key facts: H(Y|X) ≥ 0 always; H(Y|X) = 0 iff Y = f(X) for some function f (Y is determined by X); H(Y|X) = H(Y) iff X ⊥ Y.

The fundamental inequality H(Y|X) ≤ H(Y) — conditioning reduces entropy — follows from the non-negativity of mutual information. Intuitively, knowing X can only decrease (or leave unchanged) our uncertainty about Y; it can never increase it.
Chain Rule for Entropy

The chain rule H(X,Y) = H(X) + H(Y|X) is the information-theoretic analogue of the probability chain rule p(x,y) = p(x)·p(y|x). It extends to n variables: H(X₁,...,Xₙ) = Σᵢ H(Xᵢ | X₁,...,Xᵢ₋₁), where H(X₁|∅) = H(X₁). Each term represents the additional information in Xᵢ given all previous variables.

import numpy as np

def entropy_bits(p):
    p = np.asarray(p, dtype=float)
    p = p[p > 0]
    return -np.sum(p * np.log2(p))

def joint_entropy(pxy):
    pxy = np.asarray(pxy, dtype=float)
    flat = pxy.flatten()
    flat = flat[flat > 0]
    return -np.sum(flat * np.log2(flat))

def mutual_information(pxy):
    pxy = np.asarray(pxy, dtype=float)
    HX  = entropy_bits(pxy.sum(axis=1))
    HY  = entropy_bits(pxy.sum(axis=0))
    HXY = joint_entropy(pxy)
    return HX + HY - HXY

# Verify chain rule: H(X,Y) = H(X) + H(Y|X)
pxy = np.array([[0.3, 0.05, 0.05],
                [0.05, 0.3, 0.05],
                [0.05, 0.05, 0.1]])

HXY = joint_entropy(pxy)
HX  = entropy_bits(pxy.sum(axis=1))
HYgX = HXY - HX   # H(Y|X) = H(X,Y) - H(X)
HY  = entropy_bits(pxy.sum(axis=0))

print("Chain rule verification:")
print(f"  H(X)        = {HX:.4f} bits")
print(f"  H(Y|X)      = {HYgX:.4f} bits")
print(f"  H(X)+H(Y|X) = {HX+HYgX:.4f} bits")
print(f"  H(X,Y)      = {HXY:.4f} bits  (should match)")

I = mutual_information(pxy)
print(f"\nMutual Information I(X;Y):")
print(f"  I(X;Y) = H(Y) - H(Y|X) = {HY:.4f} - {HYgX:.4f} = {I:.4f} bits")
print(f"  I(X;Y) = H(X) + H(Y) - H(X,Y) = {HX+HY-HXY:.4f} bits  (consistent)")
print(f"  H(Y|X) <= H(Y): {HYgX:.4f} <= {HY:.4f}  => {HYgX <= HY}")
Demonstrating That Conditioning Reduces Entropy

import numpy as np

def entropy_bits(p):
    p = np.asarray(p, dtype=float)
    p = p[p > 0]
    return -np.sum(p * np.log2(p))

def joint_entropy_2d(pxy):
    pxy = np.asarray(pxy).flatten()
    pxy = pxy[pxy > 0]
    return -np.sum(pxy * np.log2(pxy))

def run_example(name, pxy):
    pxy = np.asarray(pxy, dtype=float)
    HX   = entropy_bits(pxy.sum(axis=1))
    HY   = entropy_bits(pxy.sum(axis=0))
    HXY  = joint_entropy_2d(pxy)
    HYgX = HXY - HX
    reduced = HY - HYgX
    print(f"  {name}: H(Y)={HY:.3f}  H(Y|X)={HYgX:.3f}  reduction={reduced:.3f} bits")

# Case 1: X and Y independent
run_example("Independent    ", np.outer([0.5,0.5],[0.7,0.3]))

# Case 2: moderate correlation
run_example("Correlated     ", [[0.4,0.1],[0.1,0.4]])

# Case 3: Y = f(X) (deterministic)
run_example("Y=f(X) determin", [[0.6,0.0],[0.0,0.4]])

# Case 4: near-deterministic
run_example("Near-determ    ", [[0.59,0.01],[0.01,0.39]])

print("\nConclusion: H(Y|X) <= H(Y) in all cases; equality iff independent.")
Entropy of Functions and Data Processing

For any deterministic function f, H(f(X)) ≤ H(X). Deterministic processing can only reduce or preserve entropy; it can never increase it. This is a special case of the data processing inequality: if X → Y → Z forms a Markov chain, then I(X;Z) ≤ I(X;Y). Information cannot be created from nothing — any transformation of data can only discard or preserve information, never generate new information about the original variable.

import numpy as np

def entropy_bits(p):
    p = np.asarray(p, dtype=float)
    p = p[p > 0]
    return -np.sum(p * np.log2(p))

def entropy_of_function(p_x, f_values):
    """H(f(X)) where f maps outcome index to f_values."""
    p_x = np.asarray(p_x, dtype=float)
    f_vals = np.asarray(f_values)
    # Accumulate probability for each unique output value
    from collections import defaultdict
    p_fx = defaultdict(float)
    for px, fx in zip(p_x, f_vals):
        p_fx[fx] += px
    return entropy_bits(list(p_fx.values()))

# X uniform over {0,1,2,3,4,5}
p_x = np.ones(6) / 6
H_X = entropy_bits(p_x)

# f1: identity (f preserves all info)
H_f1 = entropy_of_function(p_x, [0,1,2,3,4,5])

# f2: parity (maps to {even, odd}) - many-to-one
H_f2 = entropy_of_function(p_x, [0,1,0,1,0,1])

# f3: constant function - loses all info
H_f3 = entropy_of_function(p_x, [0,0,0,0,0,0])

# f4: square mod 3
H_f4 = entropy_of_function(p_x, [(x**2) % 3 for x in range(6)])

print(f"H(X) = {H_X:.4f} bits  (X uniform over 6 outcomes)")
print(f"H(f1(X)) = {H_f1:.4f} bits  [identity: preserves all info]")
print(f"H(f2(X)) = {H_f2:.4f} bits  [parity: 1 bit retained]")
print(f"H(f4(X)) = {H_f4:.4f} bits  [x² mod 3: partial info]")
print(f"H(f3(X)) = {H_f3:.4f} bits  [constant: all info lost]")
print("\nVerified: H(f(X)) <= H(X) for all f.")

0 iff X⊥Y; = H(X) if Y=f(X) injective
= H(X) if f injective; 0 if f constant

blocks.content: Multivariate Chain Rule

The multivariate chain rule H(X₁,...,Xₙ) = Σᵢ H(Xᵢ|X₁,...,Xᵢ₋₁) has a beautiful interpretation: to describe n variables, describe the first one (H(X₁) bits), then describe the second given the first (H(X₂|X₁) bits), and so on. The ordering does not matter — the total is the same regardless of which variable we condition on first. This is because H(X,Y) = H(X) + H(Y|X) = H(Y) + H(X|Y).

blocks.title: Subadditivity via Chain Rule
blocks.content: Subadditivity H(X,Y) ≤ H(X) + H(Y) follows immediately from H(Y|X) ≤ H(Y): H(X,Y) = H(X) + H(Y|X) ≤ H(X) + H(Y). Equality holds iff I(X;Y)=0, i.e., X and Y are independent.
Summary of Key Inequalities

items: H(X,Y) = H(X) + H(Y|X)  [chain rule]
H(X,Y) ≤ H(X) + H(Y)  [subadditivity; equality iff independent]
H(Y|X) ≤ H(Y)  [conditioning reduces entropy; equality iff independent]
H(Y|X) ≥ 0  [non-negativity]
H(Y|X) = 0 iff Y = f(X) deterministically
H(f(X)) ≤ H(X) for any function f
I(X;Y) = H(Y) - H(Y|X) ≥ 0  [non-negativity of mutual information]
H(X₁,...,Xₙ) ≤ Σᵢ H(Xᵢ)  [general subadditivity]

blocks.content: Joint and conditional entropy form the foundation for all multi-variable information measures. Mutual information, the most important dependency measure in information theory, is simply the reduction in entropy from conditioning: I(X;Y) = H(Y) - H(Y|X). These concepts extend naturally to KL divergence, channel capacity, and the information bottleneck principle.

title: Cross-Entropy as a Loss Function and MLE Connection
description: Cross-entropy H(p,q) = H(p) + KL(p‖q) connects data compression to statistical estimation. Covers binary and categorical cross-entropy, why minimizing cross-entropy is equivalent to MLE, gradients vs MSE, label smoothing, temperature scaling, and perplexity.

blocks.content: Cross-entropy is the workhorse loss function for classification in modern machine learning. Its ubiquity is not accidental — it has a deep information-theoretic justification connecting data compression, statistical estimation, and maximum likelihood. Understanding cross-entropy from first principles illuminates why it outperforms alternatives like MSE for probabilistic outputs.
Cross-Entropy Defined

Given a true distribution p and a model distribution q over the same support, the cross-entropy H(p,q) = -Σ_x p(x) log q(x) measures the average number of bits needed to encode samples from p using a code optimized for q. If the model q perfectly matches p, then H(p,q) = H(p) — we achieve the Shannon entropy limit. Any mismatch between p and q increases the required bits by exactly KL(p‖q).

blocks.title: Decomposition: Cross-Entropy = Entropy + KL Divergence
blocks.content: H(p,q) = H(p) + KL(p‖q). Since H(p) is fixed (the true distribution does not depend on our model), minimizing H(p,q) over model parameters θ is identical to minimizing KL(p‖q). This is why cross-entropy is the natural loss for probabilistic models.
Connection to Maximum Likelihood Estimation

Minimizing cross-entropy H(p_data, q_θ) is exactly equivalent to Maximum Likelihood Estimation (MLE). The empirical distribution p_data puts mass 1/N on each observed sample xᵢ. Then H(p_data, q_θ) = -(1/N) Σᵢ log q_θ(xᵢ) = -mean log-likelihood. Minimizing this is the same as maximizing the log-likelihood Σᵢ log q_θ(xᵢ). MLE, cross-entropy minimization, and KL divergence minimization are three views of the same operation.

import numpy as np
import torch
import torch.nn as nn

def binary_cross_entropy_scratch(y_true, y_pred, eps=1e-9):
    """Binary cross-entropy: H = -[y log ŷ + (1-y) log(1-ŷ)]"""
    y_pred = np.clip(y_pred, eps, 1 - eps)
    return -np.mean(y_true * np.log(y_pred) + (1 - y_true) * np.log(1 - y_pred))

def categorical_cross_entropy_scratch(y_true_onehot, y_pred_probs, eps=1e-9):
    """Categorical cross-entropy: H = -Σ p(k) log q(k)"""
    y_pred_probs = np.clip(y_pred_probs, eps, 1)
    return -np.mean(np.sum(y_true_onehot * np.log(y_pred_probs), axis=1))

# Binary cross-entropy comparison
y_true = np.array([1., 0., 1., 1., 0.])
y_pred = np.array([0.9, 0.1, 0.8, 0.6, 0.3])

bce_scratch = binary_cross_entropy_scratch(y_true, y_pred)
bce_torch = nn.BCELoss()(
    torch.tensor(y_pred, dtype=torch.float32),
    torch.tensor(y_true, dtype=torch.float32)
).item()
print(f"Binary CE (scratch): {bce_scratch:.6f}")
print(f"Binary CE (torch):   {bce_torch:.6f}")

# Categorical cross-entropy comparison
K = 3
y_oh = np.array([[1,0,0],[0,1,0],[0,0,1],[1,0,0]])
y_pr = np.array([[0.8,0.1,0.1],[0.1,0.7,0.2],[0.05,0.15,0.8],[0.6,0.2,0.2]])
cce_scratch = categorical_cross_entropy_scratch(y_oh, y_pr)
# torch expects logits → convert via log
cce_torch = nn.NLLLoss()(
    torch.tensor(np.log(np.clip(y_pr, 1e-9, 1)), dtype=torch.float32),
    torch.tensor([0,1,2,0])
).item()
print(f"\nCategorical CE (scratch): {cce_scratch:.6f}")
print(f"Categorical CE (torch):   {cce_torch:.6f}")
Why Cross-Entropy Beats MSE for Classification

For binary classification with a sigmoid output, the gradient of MSE w.r.t. the logit z is (ŷ - y) · σ(z)(1-σ(z)). When ŷ ≈ 0 or ŷ ≈ 1, the sigmoid derivative σ(z)(1-σ(z)) ≈ 0, causing gradient saturation — learning slows or stops even when the prediction is confidently wrong. Cross-entropy avoids this: its gradient w.r.t. z is simply (ŷ - y), a clean linear signal that is large when the model is wrong and small when it is right.

import numpy as np
import torch
import torch.nn as nn

def sigmoid(z):
    return 1 / (1 + np.exp(-z))

# Compare gradients of MSE vs Cross-Entropy w.r.t. logit z
y_true = 1.0
z_values = np.linspace(-6, 6, 200)

y_hat = sigmoid(z_values)

# MSE gradient: d/dz [(y_hat - y)^2] = 2*(y_hat - y) * y_hat*(1-y_hat)
mse_grad = 2 * (y_hat - y_true) * y_hat * (1 - y_hat)

# BCE gradient: d/dz [-y log y_hat - (1-y) log(1-y_hat)] = y_hat - y
bce_grad = y_hat - y_true

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(12, 4))

axes[0].plot(z_values, np.abs(mse_grad), label='|MSE grad|', color='tomato')
axes[0].plot(z_values, np.abs(bce_grad), label='|BCE grad|', color='steelblue')
axes[0].set_xlabel('Logit z'); axes[0].set_ylabel('|Gradient|')
axes[0].set_title('Gradient Magnitude: MSE vs BCE')
axes[0].legend(); axes[0].grid(alpha=0.3)

axes[1].plot(z_values, y_hat, color='green', label='sigmoid(z)')
axes[1].set_xlabel('Logit z'); axes[1].set_ylabel('ŷ = σ(z)')
axes[1].set_title('Sigmoid Output')
axes[1].legend(); axes[1].grid(alpha=0.3)

plt.tight_layout()
plt.savefig('bce_vs_mse_grad.png', dpi=150)
print("Gradient at z=-5 (very wrong prediction):")
idx = np.argmin(np.abs(z_values + 5))
print(f"  MSE gradient: {mse_grad[idx]:.6f}  (saturated)")
print(f"  BCE gradient: {bce_grad[idx]:.6f}  (clear signal)")
Label Smoothing

Label smoothing replaces hard one-hot targets with soft targets: p'(k) = (1-α)·1[k=y] + α/K, where α is the smoothing parameter (typically 0.1) and K is the number of classes. This prevents the model from becoming overconfident (assigning probability ≈ 1 to the true class), improves calibration, and often improves generalization. The modified cross-entropy loss is H(p', q) where p' is the smoothed distribution.

import numpy as np
import torch
import torch.nn as nn
import torch.nn.functional as F

def label_smoothing_loss(logits, targets, num_classes, smoothing=0.1):
    """
    Label smoothing cross-entropy loss.
    logits: (N, K) tensor
    targets: (N,) integer tensor
    """
    N, K = logits.shape
    log_probs = F.log_softmax(logits, dim=-1)
    # Hard target loss
    hard_loss = F.nll_loss(log_probs, targets, reduction='mean')
    # Smooth loss: uniform over all classes
    smooth_loss = -log_probs.mean(dim=-1).mean()
    return (1 - smoothing) * hard_loss + smoothing * smooth_loss

def calibration_summary(probs, labels):
    """Simple calibration: compare avg confidence vs accuracy."""
    preds = np.argmax(probs, axis=1)
    acc = (preds == labels).mean()
    confidence = probs[np.arange(len(labels)), preds].mean()
    return acc, confidence

np.random.seed(42)
N, K = 1000, 10

# Simulate overconfident model (no smoothing)
logits_raw = torch.randn(N, K) * 3
logits_t   = torch.randn(N, K) * 3
targets    = torch.randint(0, K, (N,))

loss_plain  = nn.CrossEntropyLoss()(logits_raw, targets)
loss_smooth = label_smoothing_loss(logits_t, targets, K, smoothing=0.1)

probs_plain  = F.softmax(logits_raw, dim=-1).detach().numpy()
probs_smooth = F.softmax(logits_t,   dim=-1).detach().numpy()
labels_np    = targets.numpy()

acc_p, conf_p = calibration_summary(probs_plain, labels_np)
acc_s, conf_s = calibration_summary(probs_smooth, labels_np)

print(f"Plain CE:         loss={loss_plain.item():.4f}  acc={acc_p:.3f}  avg_conf={conf_p:.3f}")
print(f"Smoothed CE:      loss={loss_smooth.item():.4f}  acc={acc_s:.3f}  avg_conf={conf_s:.3f}")
print(f"Calibration gap (|conf-acc|): plain={abs(conf_p-acc_p):.3f}  smooth={abs(conf_s-acc_s):.3f}")
Temperature Scaling for Calibration

Temperature scaling adjusts the sharpness of a trained model's softmax output without retraining: softmax(z/T). T > 1 softens the distribution (reduces overconfidence); T < 1 sharpens it. Optimal T is found by minimizing cross-entropy on a held-out calibration set. This is a popular post-hoc calibration technique introduced by Guo et al. (2017) that preserves accuracy while improving probability calibration.

import numpy as np
import torch
import torch.nn.functional as F
from scipy.optimize import minimize_scalar

def temperature_scaled_probs(logits, T):
    return F.softmax(torch.tensor(logits, dtype=torch.float32) / T, dim=-1).numpy()

def cross_entropy_loss_np(probs, targets):
    """NLL / cross-entropy given probability arrays."""
    eps = 1e-9
    return -np.mean(np.log(probs[np.arange(len(targets)), targets] + eps))

np.random.seed(0)
N, K = 500, 5
logits = np.random.randn(N, K) * 4  # overconfident logits
targets = np.random.randint(0, K, N)

# Calibrate on full set (in practice use validation set)
def neg_nll(T):
    probs = temperature_scaled_probs(logits, T)
    return cross_entropy_loss_np(probs, targets)

result = minimize_scalar(neg_nll, bounds=(0.01, 10.0), method='bounded')
T_opt = result.x

for T in [0.5, 1.0, T_opt, 2.0, 4.0]:
    probs = temperature_scaled_probs(logits, T)
    loss = cross_entropy_loss_np(probs, targets)
    avg_conf = probs.max(axis=1).mean()
    acc = (probs.argmax(axis=1) == targets).mean()
    print(f"T={T:.2f}: CE={loss:.4f}  avg_conf={avg_conf:.3f}  acc={acc:.3f}")
print(f"\nOptimal T = {T_opt:.4f}")
Perplexity

Perplexity is defined as 2^H(p,q) (bits) or exp(H(p,q)) (nats), i.e., the exponentiation of cross-entropy. For a language model with cross-entropy loss L nats per token, perplexity = exp(L). It measures how 'surprised' the model is on average — a perplexity of k means the model is as uncertain as if it were choosing uniformly from k equally likely options. Lower perplexity is better. A unigram model on English text has perplexity ~1000; GPT-4 achieves ~10-20 on standard benchmarks.

blocks.title: MLE, KL, and Cross-Entropy Are the Same
blocks.content: arg min_θ H(p_data, q_θ) = arg min_θ KL(p_data‖q_θ) = arg max_θ Σᵢ log q_θ(xᵢ). These three optimization problems have identical solutions. This equivalence is why cross-entropy is the natural loss for any model that outputs a probability distribution.
Summary

items: H(p,q) = H(p) + KL(p‖q): cross-entropy decomposes into irreducible entropy plus KL divergence
Minimizing H(p,q) over model parameters θ is identical to MLE
Binary cross-entropy gradient w.r.t. logit: (σ(z) - y) — clean, no saturation
MSE gradient for classification saturates near confident-but-wrong predictions
Label smoothing (α ≈ 0.1) improves calibration and reduces overconfidence
Temperature scaling post-hoc calibration: find T* minimizing CE on validation set
Perplexity = exp(H(p,q)): interpretable as effective vocabulary size under the model

blocks.content: Cross-entropy is not just an arbitrary loss — it is the principled information-theoretic choice for any task where the model outputs a probability distribution. Its connection to MLE and KL divergence makes it the correct objective for learning probabilistic models, and understanding this connection illuminates decisions like label smoothing, temperature scaling, and the design of calibrated systems.

title: KL Divergence — Asymmetry and Forward vs Reverse
description: KL divergence KL(P‖Q) measures the information cost of using model Q to encode data from P. Covers non-negativity via Jensen's inequality, the critical asymmetry, forward (inclusive) vs reverse (mode-seeking) KL, applications in VAEs, MLE, RLHF, and variational inference.

blocks.content: Kullback-Leibler divergence is one of the most important quantities in statistics, information theory, and machine learning. It measures how much one probability distribution differs from another, and its asymmetry — KL(P‖Q) ≠ KL(Q‖P) in general — is not a bug but a feature: each direction captures fundamentally different behaviour when approximating distributions.
Definition and Non-Negativity

For discrete distributions P and Q over the same support, KL(P‖Q) = Σ_x p(x) log(p(x)/q(x)). This can be read as the extra bits per symbol when encoding data from P using a code optimized for Q, rather than the optimal code for P. KL(P‖Q) ≥ 0 always (Gibbs' inequality), with equality iff P = Q everywhere. Proof: by Jensen's inequality applied to the convex function -log, -KL(P‖Q) = Σ p(x) log(q(x)/p(x)) ≤ log Σ p(x)·(q(x)/p(x)) = log 1 = 0.

blocks.title: KL Is Not a Distance
blocks.content: KL divergence is not a metric. It violates symmetry (KL(P‖Q) ≠ KL(Q‖P) in general) and the triangle inequality. It is undefined when Q(x)=0 but P(x)>0 (the convention is KL = +∞ in this case). Use Jensen-Shannon divergence when a symmetric, bounded measure is needed.

import numpy as np
from scipy.special import kl_div
from scipy.stats import entropy as scipy_entropy

def kl_divergence(p, q, eps=1e-12):
    """
    KL(P‖Q) = Σ p(x) log(p(x)/q(x)).
    Returns +inf if q(x)=0 and p(x)>0.
    """
    p = np.asarray(p, dtype=float)
    q = np.asarray(q, dtype=float)
    # Find support where p > 0
    mask = p > 0
    if np.any(q[mask] == 0):
        return np.inf
    return np.sum(p[mask] * np.log(p[mask] / (q[mask] + eps)))

# Demonstrate asymmetry
p = np.array([0.6, 0.3, 0.1])
q = np.array([0.2, 0.5, 0.3])

kl_pq = kl_divergence(p, q)
kl_qp = kl_divergence(q, p)

print(f"KL(P‖Q) = {kl_pq:.4f} nats")
print(f"KL(Q‖P) = {kl_qp:.4f} nats")
print(f"Asymmetric: {not np.isclose(kl_pq, kl_qp)}")

# Verify with scipy
print(f"Scipy KL(P‖Q) = {scipy_entropy(p, q):.4f} nats  (matches: {np.isclose(kl_pq, scipy_entropy(p, q))})")

# KL = 0 iff P = Q
print(f"\nKL(P‖P) = {kl_divergence(p, p):.6f}  (should be 0)")

# KL blows up when Q has zero where P has mass
q_zero = np.array([0.5, 0.5, 0.0])
print(f"KL(P‖Q) when Q has zero where P>0: {kl_divergence(p, q_zero)}")  # inf
Forward KL vs Reverse KL — The Critical Difference

Forward KL (also called 'inclusive' or 'I-projection'): minimize KL(p_true ‖ q_approx) over q. Because log(p/q) → -∞ when q → 0 but p > 0, the loss is infinite unless q covers all modes of p. This forces q to be broad — it must place mass everywhere that p does, even if p is multimodal. The result is often a smeared-out, mean-seeking approximation.

Reverse KL (also called 'exclusive' or 'M-projection'): minimize KL(q_approx ‖ p_true) over q. Because we weight by q, when q(x) → 0 there is no penalty even if p(x) > 0. This allows q to ignore modes of p entirely. The optimizer concentrates q on one mode of p (mode-seeking behaviour), fitting that mode well while ignoring others.

import numpy as np
from scipy.optimize import minimize
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

# Target: bimodal distribution (mixture of two Gaussians on discrete grid)
x = np.linspace(-5, 5, 300)
dx = x[1] - x[0]

def gaussian(x, mu, sigma):
    return np.exp(-0.5 * ((x - mu) / sigma) ** 2) / (sigma * np.sqrt(2 * np.pi))

# True distribution: bimodal
p = 0.5 * gaussian(x, -2, 0.5) + 0.5 * gaussian(x, 2, 0.5)
p = p / (p.sum() * dx)  # normalize
p_discrete = p * dx    # discrete probabilities

def fit_gaussian_approx(target_kl):
    """Fit N(mu, sigma) to bimodal p by minimizing forward or reverse KL."""
    def forward_kl(params):  # KL(p_true || q)
        mu, log_sigma = params
        sigma = np.exp(log_sigma)
        q = gaussian(x, mu, sigma)
        q = q / (q.sum() * dx)
        q_d = q * dx
        q_d = np.clip(q_d, 1e-12, None)
        return np.sum(p_discrete * np.log(np.clip(p_discrete, 1e-12, None) / q_d))

    def reverse_kl(params):  # KL(q || p_true)
        mu, log_sigma = params
        sigma = np.exp(log_sigma)
        q = gaussian(x, mu, sigma)
        q = q / (q.sum() * dx)
        q_d = np.clip(q * dx, 1e-12, None)
        p_d = np.clip(p_discrete, 1e-12, None)
        return np.sum(q_d * np.log(q_d / p_d))

    obj = forward_kl if target_kl == 'forward' else reverse_kl
    result = minimize(obj, [0.0, 0.0], method='Nelder-Mead')
    mu, log_sigma = result.x
    return mu, np.exp(log_sigma)

mu_fwd, sig_fwd = fit_gaussian_approx('forward')
mu_rev, sig_rev = fit_gaussian_approx('reverse')

print(f"Forward KL fit:  mu={mu_fwd:.3f}, sigma={sig_fwd:.3f}  (mean-seeking, wide)")
print(f"Reverse KL fit:  mu={mu_rev:.3f}, sigma={sig_rev:.3f}  (mode-seeking, narrow)")
KL in Variational Inference and VAEs

Variational Autoencoders (VAEs) minimize the negative ELBO: L = E_q[log p(x|z)] - KL(q(z|x) ‖ p(z)). The KL term is between the approximate posterior q(z|x) (encoder) and the prior p(z) (typically N(0,I)). This is the reverse KL KL(q‖p), which encourages mode-seeking behaviour — the encoder learns to concentrate on specific regions of latent space rather than spreading probability mass everywhere.

import numpy as np
import torch
import torch.nn as nn

# KL divergence between two Gaussians: closed form
# KL(N(mu1, sigma1^2) || N(mu2, sigma2^2))
def kl_gaussians(mu1, logvar1, mu2=0.0, logvar2=0.0):
    """
    Closed-form KL between two diagonal Gaussians.
    Default: KL(q || N(0,I)) used in VAE ELBO.
    """
    var1 = torch.exp(logvar1)
    var2 = torch.exp(torch.tensor(logvar2))
    kl = 0.5 * (logvar2 - logvar1 + var1 / var2
                + (mu1 - mu2) ** 2 / var2 - 1)
    return kl.sum(dim=-1).mean()

# Simulate VAE encoder output for a batch
torch.manual_seed(42)
batch_size, latent_dim = 32, 8
mu     = torch.randn(batch_size, latent_dim) * 0.5
logvar = torch.randn(batch_size, latent_dim) * 0.3 - 1  # log-variance

kl_loss = kl_gaussians(mu, logvar)

# VAE reparameterization trick
eps = torch.randn_like(mu)
z   = mu + torch.exp(0.5 * logvar) * eps

# Reconstruction loss placeholder (assume binary input)
recon_loss = nn.BCELoss()(torch.sigmoid(z), torch.rand_like(z))

elbo = recon_loss + kl_loss
print(f"VAE ELBO components (batch of {batch_size}):")
print(f"  Reconstruction loss: {recon_loss.item():.4f}")
print(f"  KL(q‖p) loss:        {kl_loss.item():.4f}")
print(f"  Total -ELBO:          {elbo.item():.4f}")
print(f"  Reparameterized z shape: {z.shape}")
KL in RLHF and Language Model Alignment

Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF) uses a KL penalty to keep the policy π_θ close to a reference policy π_ref: L = -E[r(x)] + β·KL(π_θ ‖ π_ref). The KL term prevents the policy from deviating too far from the pretrained model (reward hacking, mode collapse). This is a reverse KL: KL(π_θ ‖ π_ref), penalizing the policy for placing mass where the reference has low probability.

import numpy as np
import torch
import torch.nn.functional as F

def kl_penalty_rlhf(logits_policy, logits_ref, beta=0.01):
    """
    KL penalty used in RLHF: beta * KL(pi_theta || pi_ref).
    logits_policy, logits_ref: (batch, vocab_size)
    """
    log_p = F.log_softmax(logits_policy, dim=-1)
    log_r = F.log_softmax(logits_ref,    dim=-1)
    # KL(policy || ref) = Σ p * (log p - log r)
    kl = (log_p.exp() * (log_p - log_r)).sum(dim=-1)  # (batch,)
    return beta * kl.mean()

torch.manual_seed(1)
batch, vocab = 16, 50257  # GPT-2 vocab size

# Reference model (frozen)
logits_ref    = torch.randn(batch, vocab)
# Policy slightly shifted from reference
logits_policy = logits_ref + torch.randn(batch, vocab) * 0.5
# Strongly shifted policy (would get large KL penalty)
logits_drifted = logits_ref + torch.randn(batch, vocab) * 3.0

for name, logits in [("aligned policy", logits_policy),
                     ("drifted policy", logits_drifted)]:
    kl_pen = kl_penalty_rlhf(logits, logits_ref, beta=0.01)
    kl_raw = kl_penalty_rlhf(logits, logits_ref, beta=1.0)
    print(f"{name}: KL = {kl_raw.item():.4f} nats,  penalty (β=0.01) = {kl_pen.item():.4f}")

rows: KL = +∞ — forces Q to cover P's support
No penalty — Q can ignore modes of P
No penalty — Q can be nonzero where P=0
Q spreads to cover all modes of P
Q concentrates on one mode of P
VAE encoder, variational inference, RLHF KL penalty
Yes: Q must cover P's support
No: Q can have smaller support than P

blocks.content: JS Divergence and f-Divergences

The Jensen-Shannon divergence JSD(P,Q) = (1/2)KL(P‖M) + (1/2)KL(Q‖M) where M=(P+Q)/2 is a symmetrized, bounded variant. Both KL and JSD belong to the family of f-divergences: D_f(P‖Q) = Σ q(x) f(p(x)/q(x)) for a convex function f with f(1)=0. KL uses f(t) = t log t; reverse KL uses f(t) = -log t; JSD uses f(t) = t log(2t/(t+1)) + log(2/(t+1)).

blocks.title: MLE = Minimizing Forward KL
blocks.content: arg max_θ Σᵢ log q_θ(xᵢ) = arg min_θ KL(p_data ‖ q_θ). Maximum likelihood estimation is forward KL minimization — it forces the model to cover all the data, not just fit one cluster. This is why MLE with flexible models tends to produce broad, calibrated distributions.

KL divergence is the fundamental measure of discrepancy between probability distributions. Its asymmetry encodes two completely different optimization objectives — forward KL for inclusive coverage (MLE, cross-entropy training) and reverse KL for mode concentration (VAEs, variational inference, RLHF). Choosing the wrong direction leads to pathological behaviour: mode averaging or mode dropping.

title: Jensen-Shannon Divergence
description: JSD(P,Q) = (1/2)KL(P‖M) + (1/2)KL(Q‖M) is the symmetric, bounded sibling of KL divergence. Covers its derivation from KL, the metric property of √JSD, the GAN connection, why disjoint supports break GAN training, the Wasserstein fix, and practical dataset comparison.

blocks.content: The Jensen-Shannon divergence addresses two critical limitations of KL divergence: asymmetry and unboundedness. By symmetrizing via the mixture distribution M=(P+Q)/2, JSD is symmetric, always finite (even for distributions with disjoint supports), and its square root is a proper metric. These properties make it the natural choice for comparing datasets and understanding GAN training dynamics.
Definition and Derivation

The Jensen-Shannon divergence between P and Q is JSD(P‖Q) = (1/2)·KL(P‖M) + (1/2)·KL(Q‖M), where M = (P+Q)/2 is the mixture (midpoint) distribution. Expanding: JSD(P,Q) = H(M) - (1/2)H(P) - (1/2)H(Q), where H denotes Shannon entropy. This shows JSD as the excess entropy of the mixture over the average entropy of the components — a measure of how 'different' P and Q are.

blocks.title: JSD Bounds
blocks.content: 0 ≤ JSD(P,Q) ≤ log 2 nats (or 0 ≤ JSD ≤ 1 bit when using log base 2). JSD = 0 iff P = Q everywhere. JSD = log 2 nats (= 1 bit) iff P and Q have completely disjoint supports. These tight bounds make JSD interpretable as a fraction of maximum possible divergence.

import numpy as np
from scipy.stats import entropy as scipy_entropy

def jsd(p, q, base=2):
    """
    Jensen-Shannon divergence.
    Returns value in bits (base=2) or nats (base=e).
    JSD(P,Q) = 0.5 * KL(P||M) + 0.5 * KL(Q||M)  where M = (P+Q)/2
    """
    p = np.asarray(p, dtype=float)
    q = np.asarray(q, dtype=float)
    p = p / p.sum()
    q = q / q.sum()
    m = 0.5 * (p + q)
    # scipy entropy computes KL(P||Q) = sum p log(p/q) in nats
    kl_pm = scipy_entropy(p, m)
    kl_qm = scipy_entropy(q, m)
    jsd_nats = 0.5 * kl_pm + 0.5 * kl_qm
    if base == 2:
        return jsd_nats / np.log(2)
    return jsd_nats

# Verify symmetry
p = np.array([0.5, 0.3, 0.15, 0.05])
q = np.array([0.1, 0.4, 0.4,  0.1])

jsd_pq = jsd(p, q)
jsd_qp = jsd(q, p)
print(f"JSD(P,Q) = {jsd_pq:.6f} bits")
print(f"JSD(Q,P) = {jsd_qp:.6f} bits")
print(f"Symmetric: {np.isclose(jsd_pq, jsd_qp)}")
print(f"Bounded [0,1]: {0 <= jsd_pq <= 1}")
print(f"sqrt(JSD) = {np.sqrt(jsd_pq):.4f}  (a valid metric)")

# JSD = 1 bit for completely disjoint supports
p_disj = np.array([1.0, 0.0])
q_disj = np.array([0.0, 1.0])
print(f"\nDisjoint supports: JSD = {jsd(p_disj, q_disj):.4f} bits  (should be 1.0)")
print(f"Identical:          JSD = {jsd(p, p):.4f} bits  (should be 0.0)")
JSD is Finite for Disjoint Supports — Unlike KL

KL divergence blows up to infinity when the distributions have non-overlapping supports: if P(x)>0 but Q(x)=0, then log(P(x)/Q(x)) = +∞. JSD is immune to this because the mixture M=(P+Q)/2 always has support covering both P and Q, so M(x)>0 wherever either P(x)>0 or Q(x)>0. This makes JSD numerically stable and meaningful even for distributions concentrated on entirely separate parts of the space.

import numpy as np
from scipy.stats import entropy as scipy_entropy

def kl_safe(p, q):
    """KL(P‖Q) = +inf if Q has zeros where P has mass."""
    p = np.asarray(p, dtype=float)
    q = np.asarray(q, dtype=float)
    mask = p > 0
    if np.any(q[mask] == 0):
        return float('inf')
    return scipy_entropy(p, q)

def jsd(p, q):
    p = np.asarray(p, dtype=float) / np.sum(p)
    q = np.asarray(q, dtype=float) / np.sum(q)
    m = 0.5 * (p + q)
    return 0.5 * scipy_entropy(p, m) + 0.5 * scipy_entropy(q, m)

# Three test cases with increasing support overlap
cases = [
    ("Identical      ", [0.4,0.3,0.2,0.1], [0.4,0.3,0.2,0.1]),
    ("Partial overlap", [0.5,0.4,0.1,0.0], [0.0,0.3,0.4,0.3]),
    ("Disjoint       ", [0.6,0.4,0.0,0.0], [0.0,0.0,0.7,0.3]),
]

print(f"{'Case':<18} {'KL(P‖Q)':>12} {'KL(Q‖P)':>12} {'JSD':>10}")
print("-" * 56)
for name, p, q in cases:
    kl_fwd = kl_safe(p, q)
    kl_rev = kl_safe(q, p)
    j = jsd(p, q) / np.log(2)  # convert to bits
    kl_fwd_s = f"{kl_fwd:.4f}" if kl_fwd != float('inf') else "    inf"
    kl_rev_s = f"{kl_rev:.4f}" if kl_rev != float('inf') else "    inf"
    print(f"{name:<18} {kl_fwd_s:>12} {kl_rev_s:>12} {j:>10.4f}")
GAN Training Minimizes JSD

Goodfellow et al. (2014) showed that the original GAN minimax game — with an optimal discriminator — is equivalent to minimizing JSD(P_real ‖ P_gen) + log 4 (a constant). The generator minimizes JSD between the real data distribution and the generated distribution. This theoretical insight illuminated why GANs work, but also revealed a fundamental flaw: when P_real and P_gen have disjoint supports (common early in training), JSD = log 2 = constant, and the generator receives zero gradient.

blocks.title: Disjoint Supports = Zero GAN Gradient
blocks.content: When the real and generated distributions don't overlap (e.g., real images lie on a low-dimensional manifold far from early generator outputs), JSD reaches its maximum of log 2 nats and its gradient with respect to the generator is zero. Training stalls. This is why GAN training is notoriously unstable at the beginning and why Wasserstein GAN (WGAN) was developed as a fix.

import numpy as np
from scipy.stats import entropy as scipy_entropy
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

def jsd_bits(p, q):
    p = np.asarray(p, dtype=float) / np.sum(p)
    q = np.asarray(q, dtype=float) / np.sum(q)
    m = 0.5 * (p + q)
    return (0.5 * scipy_entropy(p, m) + 0.5 * scipy_entropy(q, m)) / np.log(2)

def kl_bits_safe(p, q):
    p = np.asarray(p, dtype=float) / np.sum(p)
    q = np.asarray(q, dtype=float) / np.sum(q)
    mask = p > 0
    if np.any(q[mask] == 0):
        return float('inf')
    return scipy_entropy(p, q) / np.log(2)

# Simulate GAN training: generated distribution gradually shifts toward real
x = np.arange(20)  # discrete space
p_real = np.zeros(20); p_real[14:18] = [0.2, 0.4, 0.3, 0.1]  # real: modes at 14-17

jsd_vals, kl_vals = [], []
shifts = np.linspace(0, 14, 50)  # generator shifts from left to right

for shift in shifts:
    center = int(shift)
    p_gen = np.zeros(20)
    for i, w in zip([center, center+1, center+2], [0.3, 0.5, 0.2]):
        if 0 <= i < 20:
            p_gen[i] += w
    p_gen = p_gen / p_gen.sum()
    jsd_vals.append(jsd_bits(p_real, p_gen))
    kl_vals.append(kl_bits_safe(p_real, p_gen))

plt.figure(figsize=(8,4))
plt.plot(shifts, jsd_vals, label='JSD (bits)', color='steelblue')
plt.plot(shifts, [min(v, 5) for v in kl_vals], label='KL(P_real‖P_gen) [clipped]', color='tomato', linestyle='--')
plt.axhline(1.0, color='gray', linestyle=':', alpha=0.5, label='JSD max = 1 bit')
plt.xlabel('Generator mean shift toward real data')
plt.ylabel('Divergence (bits)'); plt.title('JSD vs KL During GAN Training Simulation')
plt.legend(); plt.tight_layout(); plt.savefig('gan_jsd.png', dpi=150)
print(f"JSD at full overlap (disjoint→overlap): {jsd_vals[0]:.3f} → {jsd_vals[-1]:.3f} bits")
Dataset Similarity Measurement with JSD

JSD provides a principled way to measure how similar two datasets are, without requiring their supports to match. Given empirical distributions P_A and P_B (e.g., token frequency distributions, label distributions, feature histograms), JSD(P_A, P_B) ∈ [0, 1 bit] quantifies divergence. √JSD ∈ [0, 1] is a true metric. This is used for dataset shift detection, domain adaptation evaluation, and NLP corpus comparison.

import numpy as np
from scipy.stats import entropy as scipy_entropy
from collections import Counter

def jsd_bits(p, q):
    p = np.asarray(p, dtype=float)
    q = np.asarray(q, dtype=float)
    # Align supports
    assert len(p) == len(q)
    p = p / p.sum(); q = q / q.sum()
    m = 0.5 * (p + q)
    return (0.5 * scipy_entropy(p, m) + 0.5 * scipy_entropy(q, m)) / np.log(2)

def text_distribution(text, vocab_size=26):
    """Letter frequency distribution over a-z."""
    counts = np.zeros(vocab_size)
    for c in text.lower():
        if 'a' <= c <= 'z':
            counts[ord(c) - ord('a')] += 1
    return counts / counts.sum() if counts.sum() > 0 else counts

# Compare letter distributions of different text domains
corpus = {
    "English prose": "the quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog and the cat sat on the mat",
    "Scientific text": "quantum entanglement entropy eigenvalue matrix probability distribution",
    "German text":   "die schnelle braune fuchs springt ueber den faulen hund und die katze",
    "Random letters": "zqxvwkjzqxvwkjzqxvwkjzqxvwkjzqxvwkjzqxvwkj",
}

dists = {name: text_distribution(text) for name, text in corpus.items()}
names = list(dists.keys())

print("JSD (bits) between text corpora:")
print(f"{'':25}", end="")
for n in names: print(f"{n[:15]:>17}", end="")
print()
for n1 in names:
    print(f"{n1[:25]:<25}", end="")
    for n2 in names:
        j = jsd_bits(dists[n1], dists[n2])
        print(f"{j:>17.4f}", end="")
    print()
Wasserstein Distance as the Fix

Arjovsky et al. (2017) proposed Wasserstein GAN to solve the zero-gradient problem. The Wasserstein-1 distance W₁(P,Q) = inf_{γ∈Π(P,Q)} E_{(x,y)~γ}[‖x-y‖] is finite and has non-zero gradients even when P and Q have disjoint supports, because it measures the cost of 'transporting' mass from one distribution to another. WGAN trains a Lipschitz-constrained critic to estimate W₁ instead of a probability-estimating discriminator.

blocks.title: When to Use JSD vs KL vs Wasserstein
blocks.content: Use KL when comparing distributions with overlapping support for MLE or variational inference. Use JSD when you need a symmetric, bounded measure (dataset similarity, evaluation). Use Wasserstein when distributions may be disjoint and you need meaningful gradients (GAN training, optimal transport).
Summary

items: JSD(P,Q) = H((P+Q)/2) - (1/2)H(P) - (1/2)H(Q): excess entropy of the mixture
Symmetric: JSD(P,Q) = JSD(Q,P) always
Bounded: 0 ≤ JSD ≤ log 2 nats (= 1 bit with log base 2)
Always finite: even for disjoint supports (JSD = 1 bit maximum)
√JSD is a proper metric satisfying the triangle inequality
Original GAN minimizes JSD — gradient is zero for disjoint supports
WGAN fixes this by replacing JSD/KL with Wasserstein distance
Practical uses: dataset shift detection, domain comparison, NLP corpus analysis

blocks.content: Jensen-Shannon divergence bridges pure information theory and modern deep learning. Its role in the GAN objective motivated the development of optimal transport methods for generative models, and its metric properties (via √JSD) make it the principled choice for measuring distributional similarity in practice. Understanding JSD clarifies not just GANs but the broader landscape of divergence measures used throughout machine learning.
